dimension_1_problem_framing.text: The paper addresses regression-based stock market forecasting, motivated by the economic importance and difficulty of predicting financial trends, and formulates it as a time-series prediction task using historical prices augmented with technical indicators to be modeled by quantum, hybrid, and classical neural networks.

dimension_2_quantum_method.text: The authors use a custom Quantum Neural Network (QNN) regressor built from parameterized quantum circuits with angle encoding of classical stock features, a customized ansatz designed to enhance expressivity and mitigate barren plateaus, and entangling CNOT/CZ operations whose measurement outcomes produce observables for prediction. This QNN is deployed in three variants: a standalone quantum regressor and two hybrid architectures (HybridQNN1 sequential classical-to-quantum, HybridQNN2 jointly optimized quantum–classical) trained with Adam on a QULACS simulator, with experiments sweeping 3–5 qubits.

dimension_3_key_results.text: Results indicate that quantum-assisted learning can contribute to financial modeling, with the integrated hybrid HybridQNN2 consistently achieving the lowest RMSE among the quantum-enhanced methods and exhibiting narrower, more concentrated error distributions than the standalone CustomQNN, whose errors show higher variance. Increasing the qubit count to five improves accuracy for HybridQNN2, though all three quantum-based models partially track real prices only in a stable regime and fail to adapt when the market undergoes abrupt regime shifts, with predictions remaining in the initial price range. The authors also report that k-fold cross-validation provides a more generalized estimate of predictive performance across their models.

dimension_4_classical_comparison.text: Classical recurrent models (RNN, LSTM, BiLSTM, GRU) are used as benchmarks, and the authors report that these classical models continue to achieve the lowest RMSE overall, outperforming all quantum and hybrid variants. Within the quantum-enhanced set, hybridization—especially the fully integrated HybridQNN2—reduces some of the limitations observed in the standalone QNN, yielding better RMSE and tighter error distributions compared with CustomQNN.

dimension_5_stated_limitations.text: The authors highlight several limitations: classical recurrent models still outperform the quantum and hybrid approaches in RMSE, and all three quantum-based models struggle under abrupt market regime shifts, keeping predictions within the initial price range instead of adapting to new levels. They note that increasing qubit counts introduces an accuracy–efficiency trade-off, as higher qubit configurations incur longer training times. At a more fundamental level, they acknowledge that quantum circuit execution is resource-intensive and constrained by the current capabilities of NISQ hardware, indicating that practical performance and scalability are limited by present devices and the depth/encoding choices of their circuits.

dimension_6_future_work.text: Future work directions include optimizing quantum encoding schemes, reducing circuit depth, and improving noise resilience to enhance the feasibility of hybrid approaches, as well as exploring larger-scale quantum architectures and more advanced, noise-resilient quantum processors. The authors also propose extending the study to larger datasets and richer sets of technical indicators and stress that testing real-time applications directly on quantum hardware will be crucial to assess practical feasibility in financial markets.

dimension_7_novelty_claim.text: The paper claims novelty in proposing a hybrid model that seamlessly integrates custom-designed QNNs with classical deep learning architectures for stock market regression, including a purpose-built QNN regressor based on a customized ansatz and parameterized quantum circuits tailored to financial data. It further contributes two distinct hybrid optimization strategies—one sequential pipeline where a classical model performs feature extraction before a shallow quantum circuit, and one fully integrated HybridQNN2 with joint optimization under a shared loss—alongside a robust evaluation protocol involving systematic hyperparameter tuning, TimeSeriesSplit, k-fold cross-validation, and error visualizations.

dimension_8_methodological_notes.text: Methodologically, the study uses real stock market data augmented with multiple domain-specific technical indicators (RSI, MACD, ADX) and applies feature selection via SelectKBest, normalization, and time-ordered train–test splits to preserve temporal integrity. The experimental design includes classical baselines (RNN, LSTM, BiLSTM, GRU), three quantum-driven architectures, TimeSeriesSplit for sequential validation, and k-fold cross-validation, with early stopping, learning-rate scheduling, and Adam optimization under an MSE objective. The authors explicitly compare TimeSeriesSplit and k-fold, arguing that TimeSeriesSplit better respects chronology while k-fold provides a more generalized performance estimate, and they use HPC resources with a QULACS simulator to explore the impact of varying qubit counts on performance and training time.

dimension_9_miscellaneous.text: The authors emphasize that hybrid quantum–classical models are positioned as a practical pathway for bringing quantum machine learning into financial applications in the near term, motivated by the anticipated benefits of improved feature representation and learning from quantum resources, though these benefits remain exploratory in this work.
